card.hook: On a calm morning, Amber Fort shows up twice: once on its hillside and once upside down in Maota Lake. It's like getting two forts for the price of one.
card.stand_here: Head for the eastern shore of Maota Lake, below the fort, and face the fort so the slope and the water both fit in your frame. The lake lies directly below the fort, so you can't miss it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the fort and its reflection together. If you're right by the water, try 0.5x to squeeze in more shoreline, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the ramparts and gates.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line, so the fort and its reflection fill the frame and the horizon stays level.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning while the water is still. One guide says November to February is best for the reflection.
card.selfie_here: Inside the fort, stand in the second courtyard with the painted Ganesh Pol gate behind you. It's named again and again as the fort's most photographed spot. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it for the front camera, to fit more gate in. For a roomier backdrop, Jaleb Chowk, the big first courtyard, has walls and gateways around you. Check on site which way gives the best view behind you.
card.ask_someone: On the road beside Maota Lake, before you park, ask a passer-by to photograph you at the lakeside with the fort above you in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Amber Fort itself has a paid entry ticket, but the lakeside viewpoint is outside it. Check the official site before you go, and check entry details for Jaigarh Fort too if you plan to visit.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the lake, then pick the calmest one. Bonus points if the fort looks the same the right way up and upside down.
card.good_to_know: The palace is built of red sandstone and marble and has four levels, each with its own courtyard. Raja Man Singh began it and Jai Singh I expanded it in the early 1600s. The Kachwaha capital moved to Jaipur in 1727, and the fort is part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2013. Amer is about 11 km from Jaipur city, so allow time for the journey and the climb up to the fort.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the eastern shore of Maota Lake, below the fort, and face the fort so the slope and the water both fit in your frame. The lake lies directly below the fort, so you can't miss it.

card.hook: Picture 953 tiny windows staring back at you across a road full of honking autos. That's the Hawa Mahal, and it looks like a pink honeycomb that someone stood up on its end.
card.stand_here: Head for the Badi Chaupar crossroads and stand on the pavement directly opposite the facade, at the northeast corner. The Hawa Mahal is straight ahead to the north, about 2 minutes on foot away if you want to walk closer, so face north.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so all five floors fit. If traffic or people force you to stand close, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the windows and carving.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the pink stone keeps its colour against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Go before 8:00 AM. The facade faces east, so the morning sun hits it head-on, and the streets are quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Try the small traffic island or road edge directly in front of the palace at Badi Chaupar, where the facade fills the background. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and tuck the palace behind your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot, because we couldn't confirm the exact angle.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the northeast corner of the Badi Chaupar crossroads and frame the whole facade, while you use the pedestrian crossing and stand on the pavement opposite.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic is busy here, so use the pedestrian crossing, keep to the pavement, and don't stand in the carriageway for a photo.
card.challenge: Catch the whole pink front with one auto and one person at the bottom of the frame, and keep your vertical lines dead straight. Bonus points if nobody honks.
card.good_to_know: Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh built the Hawa Mahal in 1799. Its 953 small windows are called jharokhas, and they let royal ladies watch street life and festivals without being seen. They also let cool air move through the building. It's about 15 metres tall, and the top three floors are only one room wide.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Badi Chaupar crossroads and stand on the pavement directly opposite the facade, at the northeast corner. The Hawa Mahal is straight ahead to the north, about 2 minutes on foot away if you want to walk closer, so face north.

card.hook: Picture a peacock strutting across a perfectly cut lawn while a pink sandstone palace bristles with domes behind it. That's Rambagh Palace, and the roofline is the real showstopper.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, out on the palace lawns in front of the building, and face the palace so the front and side façade fill your view. Moti Dungri Fort peeks out behind on one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade and lawn in one shot. Then go to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view. Finish with 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the domes, cupolas and chhatris against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the roofline on the upper line so the domes have sky around them, then tap the pink stone and slide it a touch darker so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the pick, according to one guide. Peacocks are often out in the evening light too, which is a nice bonus.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawns of The Verandah, especially in the evening when the peacocks are out. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if you're shooting a friend, and keep the palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in front of the main façade and entrance while you stand with the domes and cupolas behind you, ideally at dusk.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working hotel, so be quiet, keep to public areas and follow staff instructions. Visitors who aren't staying can usually only get into the grounds by booking a meal or high tea, so check the official site before you go. Personal phone photos are fine in restaurant areas and public courtyards, but private or restricted areas are off limits.
card.challenge: Get a peacock walking through the foreground with the palace roofline sitting neatly on your top gridline. Patience required, peacocks don't take direction.
card.good_to_know: The palace began in 1835 as a modest garden house. By 1925 it was the main home of Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II. After independence it became India's first luxury palace hotel, and Taj Hotels has run it since 1972.

card.hook: From the shore, Jal Mahal looks like someone forgot to finish the lake and left a palace floating in it. It's a quick stop, but it's a very good one.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Amer Road lakeside promenade, at its midpoint, directly opposite the palace. Face east across the water, and the palace will be straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole palace and its reflection. Then try zoom 2x for a tighter shot with the hills squeezed in behind it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the palace on the centre line, so it and its reflection sit nicely balanced.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the wind ruffles the water. That's when you get the calmest reflection.
card.selfie_here: Head for the lakeside path by the palace and look for the 'Selfie Point' signs (one listing mentions them, so don't be shocked if they're missing). Use the front camera and keep the palace behind you, over your shoulder.

card.rules_and_safety: Stay behind the railing at the lakeside, and watch for fast traffic on Amer Road.
card.challenge: Crouch down low until the reflection fills the bottom half of your picture, then see if you can spot all four little domed pavilions on the roof.
card.good_to_know: Sawai Jai Singh built Jal Mahal around 1699 as a duck-hunting lodge, not a royal home. Maharaja Madho Singh I renovated and enlarged it in the mid-18th century. It has five storeys, but when the lake is full the lower four are underwater. You can't go inside, so it's an outside-only stop.

card.hook: You don't need a palace ticket to get a palace photo here. Climb to a rooftop in old Jaipur and the whole City Palace spreads out below you like a model set.
card.stand_here: Go up to the rooftop of The Tattoo Cafe & Lounge in the Hawa Mahal area, a short walk south-east of the palace and opposite the palace side of that area. Face north-west and you'll find the palace complex below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the rooftop and the city in one frame. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the palace buildings in the distance. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the rooftop and big sky in the picture too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the rooftops level, then tap the palace and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go early. The palace gets crowded after about 10 AM, and an early start helps whether you stay on the rooftop or go inside.
card.selfie_here: If you go into the palace, head to Pritam Niwas Chowk and stand in front of the Peacock Gate and Lotus Gate with a gate behind you. Several guides call it the favourite selfie backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the gate fills the space over your shoulder. The pink archways just inside the entrance are another popular spot, and an early visit means fewer people in your shot.
card.ask_someone: At Jaleb Chowk, the main entrance courtyard, ask someone to stand back far enough to fit the whole grand gateway, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace complex is ticketed and its photo rules vary, so check the official site first. Photography is prohibited in the Diwan-e-Khaas royal darbar and restricted in some other sections. Flash isn't allowed in the museums. A photography fee may apply on top of your ticket, and guides disagree on the amount, so ask at the counter. The cafe rooftop is the free-access option, but check there too.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole city, then zoom in and find a single courtyard or pavilion that nobody else would think to photograph.
card.good_to_know: Sawai Jai Singh II began building the City Palace soon after he moved his court to Jaipur in 1727, and the main work was finished in 1732. It mixes Mughal and Rajput styles, and part of it is still home to the Jaipur royal family today. The pink city around it is credited to Maharaja Ram Singh, who had it painted to honour a visit by the Prince of Wales.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to the rooftop of The Tattoo Cafe & Lounge in the Hawa Mahal area, a short walk south-east of the palace and opposite the palace side of that area. Face north-west and you'll find the palace complex below you.

card.hook: Picture a long, low stone wall stretched along a ridge, with all of Jaipur spread out below it. That's Nahargarh, and it's a fort that looks best when you let the hillside share the frame.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 290 m north of the subject, and face south to see the fort. From here it looks fairly small, and that's fine.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the fort and the hillside. If the walls don't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to pick out the fort against the ridge, or zoom 5x (depending on your phone) for bastions and battlements.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the phone level so the long walls don't tilt, and line the walls up along the lower or upper third with room for sky or hillside.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the stone. Around midday you'll be facing south, so the fort can be backlit and the sky washed out.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low and out to the side. Turn so the fort and hillside sit over your shoulder rather than behind your head.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a ticketed site with set opening and closing times, and entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Keep that long wall dead level on a gridline and get the whole ridge in, with the fort looking like it grew out of the hill.
card.good_to_know: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh built Nahargarh mainly in 1734 as a retreat on the ridge above the city. With Amber Fort and Jaigarh Fort, it once formed a defensive ring around Jaipur. The name means 'abode of tigers', and films like Rang De Basanti and Shuddh Desi Romance were shot here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 290 m north of the subject, and face south to see the fort. From here it looks fairly small, and that's fine.

card.hook: Here's a staircase with a shadow that really moves: about a hand's breadth every minute, slow enough to watch while you line up your shot. That's the giant sundial at Jantar Mantar, and it's wonderfully easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the base of the Vrihat Samrat Yantra, the giant sundial, and face up its staircase. The middle of the site is a little to the north-west of here.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole staircase and the sky fit in. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the engraved scales and the little cupola on top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky, then slide it a little darker so the blue stays rich and the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early, around 9 to 10 AM, when the light is warm and the shadows are long and clear. Afternoons tend to be busier with tour groups.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the open ground at the foot of the giant sundial, with the sundial rising behind you. Use the front camera, and if it has a 0.5x button, tap it to fit more of that big stone staircase over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the entrance, facing the sundial, while you pose in the scene, so the sundial and several other instruments fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Jantar Mantar is a ticketed site, so check the official site for entry, opening times and photography rules before you go. Older visitors should avoid midday in summer because of the extreme heat and lack of shade.
card.challenge: Snap the sundial's shadow now, wander off to the bowls, then come back a few minutes later and shoot it again. Spot how far it has crept?
card.good_to_know: Jantar Mantar is an open-air observatory of 19 huge stone instruments, built by Sawai Jai Singh, the founder of Jaipur, and completed in 1734. The giant sundial is 88 feet (27 m) high, and its face is angled at 27 degrees, the latitude of Jaipur. UNESCO lists the whole site as a World Heritage Site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the base of the Vrihat Samrat Yantra, the giant sundial, and face up its staircase. The middle of the site is a little to the north-west of here.

card.hook: Most people shoot Birla Mandir from the road and leave. The better picture is down by the water, where the white dome has a twin upside down in the pool.
card.stand_here: Stand at the reflection pool just inside the entrance gate, which is where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the temple so the main dome is straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the reflection. Use 0.5x from Jawahar Lal Nehru Marg to fit the whole façade with the hill behind it. Try zoom 2x or higher for the founders' statues and the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the pool's edge on the lower line, and hold your phone low and close to the water so the reflection grows.
card.best_time: Pick a calm, windless day so the water stays still. Evening is lovely too, when the temple is lit up (use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or rail). The complex is generally closed around midday, so check the hours on the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the reflection pool near the entrance gate with the temple behind you, and use the front camera. Wait for a windless moment so the dome's mirror image shows up behind your shoulder. The lawns and gardens around the temple are another good spot, with the temple in the background.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the main gate on the Jawahar Lal Nehru Marg side and ask your photographer to frame the full façade with all three domes behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine on the outer areas, gardens and steps, but not inside the prayer hall or sanctum. Don't photograph the deities, and keep flash off indoors. Visitors report the rules differently (some say photos are banned even outside), so read the signs and ask staff before you start. In summer, come early or late, because the marble gets very hot by midday.
card.challenge: Catch the dome and its reflection in one frame without a single ripple. You may have to wait for it.
card.good_to_know: Birla Mandir is also called the Lakshmi Narayan Temple, and it's dedicated to Lakshmi and Vishnu (Narayan). The B.M. Birla Foundation built it, and it opened on 22 February 1988. Marble figures on the outer walls include Christ, Buddha, Confucius and Socrates. The founders, Rukmani Devi Birla and Braj Mohan Birla, are shown in covered pavilions facing the temple with their hands folded.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the reflection pool just inside the entrance gate, which is where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the temple so the main dome is straight ahead of you.

card.hook: Picture a red sandstone wall running along a hilltop for about 3 km, like it's got somewhere to be. That's Jaigarh Fort, and from far away it looks great against the sky.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 450 m west of the subject, and face east. The ridge and its walls will stretch out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole fort on its ridge. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out ramparts and gateways. Save 0.5x for when you're up close inside the fort.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the ridge line on the lower third, so there's room for lots of sky above and the long wall doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit this view. The sun should be behind you and give the walls a warm glow.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Jaivana Cannon platform near the fort's viewpoint area and stand beside the cannon with the ramparts behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and try 0.5x to fit more in. It's the closest match we've found to a fort-behind-you spot, so check the framing when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Down by Maota Lake on the Amer side, hand your phone to someone on the lake bank and pose so Jaigarh Fort sits on the hills behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep water with you, since open areas of the fort can feel hot and windy. Check the official site before you go for entry rules.
card.challenge: Get the whole ridge wall in one shot with the horizon dead level on the gridlines. Then see if you can spot the eagle in 'Hill of Eagles'.
card.good_to_know: The fort sits on Cheel ka Teela, the Hill of Eagles, and is also called Victory Fort. It was a cannon foundry, and it's home to the Jaivana cannon, once the largest cannon on wheels in the world. Jai Singh II built palace apartments here, and the fort stands roughly 400 m above Amer Fort.

card.hook: Picture a tall central tower and dome with a wide lawn rolled out in front of it, like the building is posing for you. Albert Hall Museum really is that neat and symmetrical.
card.stand_here: Stand on the main front lawn in Ram Niwas Garden, straight on from the central entrance, and face north toward the museum. Walk back until the whole front fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole facade with the lawn at the bottom. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the tower and dome. Use 0.5x only if you walk much closer and still want the full front in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the central tower up with the middle vertical line, and keep your phone level so both sides of the building match.
card.best_time: Go around 9-10 AM for soft light on the stonework. From about 7 PM the building is lit up, but opening hours can vary, so check on the day before a night visit.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the reflecting pool directly in front of the central facade, with the museum behind you, and use the front camera (tap 0.5x if your phone offers it). Pick a still day for a mirror reflection, and check the pool is running first, since guides say it only works at times.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the main entrance gate of Ram Niwas Garden, facing north, while you stand on the lawn in front of the building so you both fit in with the whole facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed in the galleries, and phone photos inside are free. Pro, commercial, pre-wedding or filming shoots may need separate permission. Don't try to get your shot from busy traffic areas.
card.challenge: Get a perfectly symmetrical shot where the tower sits dead centre on the gridline, then see if your friends can spot any difference between the left and right halves.
card.good_to_know: This is Rajasthan's state museum and the oldest museum in the state. Samuel Swinton Jacob designed it, the foundation stone was laid in 1876 during the Prince of Wales's visit, and it opened to the public in 1887. Inside you'll find paintings, carpets, jewellery and an Egyptian mummy.

card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the front the way your eyes see it. If the pavement is narrow and the curve won't fit, go to 0.5x. For a close-up of the star shapes, try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the building's vertical lines straight, then tap the building and drag a little darker if the sky is washing out the facade.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the outside is easy to see. Early in the day is likely to mean fewer people and less traffic, and a clearer gap at the entrance.
card.selfie_here: Head into the grand entrance hall and take your selfie under the giant chandeliers, before the show starts. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the chandeliers sit over your shoulder. If the lobby is crowded, the foyer on the ramp up to the balcony is a second indoor spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the auditorium during a screening are generally not allowed, though the lobby and hallways are usually fine before or after the show. It's a working cinema, so follow its rules about photography inside.
card.challenge: Can you spot all nine stars on the outside and get them in one shot without a rickshaw photobombing?
card.good_to_know: Raj Mandir opened on 1 June 1976 and was designed by architect W. M. Namjoshi. It was the last of the 34 cinema halls he designed. The nine stars stand for the nine gemstones of the Navaratna style, a nod to the jewellery house that owns and runs the cinema.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: the best photo at Galtaji isn't of one temple. It's the whole green valley, where temple buildings and hills fold into each other and the view opens out toward Jaipur.
card.stand_here: Start at Galta Gate, on the walking path and valley edge just beyond it. From there the temple complex is about 1 km (955 m) to the east. Face down the green Aravalli valley, toward the city, with the temple hills in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of the valley, then go to 1x for a natural view toward the city. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the temple buildings and hills in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the valley fills most of the frame, and use the path or the edge of the gate in the foreground for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning tends to give softer light. It's also the sensible time to climb, since you'll want to avoid the hottest part of the day.
card.selfie_here: For a big-view selfie, climb to the terraces by the Surya Mandir at the top of the hill. Use the front camera, with the valley and temple complex below you over your shoulder. One guide describes the sunset views from those terraces as panoramic. For an easier one, stand at the edge of the Galta Kund with the pink temple building behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand a short distance back from the main Galta Ji temple entrance, so the whole temple fits in the frame, while you pose at the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Phone photos are allowed, but fee reports conflict, so check at the gate. Look for signs and ask staff before photographing inside a deity's shrine, and don't photograph people without asking. Monkeys grab phones and food, so keep your phone secure between shots and don't carry open food.
card.challenge: Can you get three layers in one frame: a path in front, temple roofs in the middle and hills folding away behind?
card.good_to_know: Galtaji is a temple complex tucked into a green valley in the hills at the edge of Jaipur. Carry on to the Surya Mandir (Sun Temple) and you get a wide panorama over the city and forts, but expect steps and a 15 to 20 minute climb. The Lower Galta Kund is a sacred tank with temple walls and trees around it, and its still water can give nice reflections.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at Galta Gate, on the walking path and valley edge just beyond it. From there the temple complex is about 1 km (955 m) to the east. Face down the green Aravalli valley, toward the city, with the temple hills in the frame.

card.hook: Picture warm sandstone and pale marble sitting in a pocket of green, right in the middle of a busy city. That calm, colourful scene is why this temple makes such a nice stop.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jai Niwas Garden, the garden behind and beside the temple building inside the City Palace complex, and face the temple. If you can't find it, follow the signs or ask staff once you're inside.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a wide shot of the whole building with the garden around it. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved stonework without walking up to the walls. Use 0.5x only if the building won't fit.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the temple's vertical edges with them so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is worth trying for softer light on the stone. Prayer times vary, so check them locally if you want the temple at its busiest or quietest.
card.selfie_here: Take it in the outer garden grounds of Jai Niwas Garden, with the sandstone and marble facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze the building in over your shoulder, and tap the screen on your face to keep it bright.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the entrance courtyard on the Jalebi Chowk side, facing the temple, so the whole facade and entrance fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the main deity and inside the sanctum are not allowed, especially during aarti. Outer courtyards and gardens are the safe bet, but guides disagree on the details, so check signs or ask staff before you raise your phone. Keep your phone away from worshippers' faces.
card.challenge: Find the spot where sandstone meets green leaves and frame it so the leaves make a border around the carving.
card.good_to_know: Govind Dev Ji is a Hindu temple for Radha and Krishna. Maharaja Jai Singh II, who founded Jaipur, brought the deities from Vrindavan in the 18th century. Its Satsang Hall holds a 2009 Guinness World Record as the world's widest concrete building, with a 119-foot roof span and no pillars, but that's inside, so you won't get it from the garden.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jai Niwas Garden, the garden behind and beside the temple building inside the City Palace complex, and face the temple. If you can't find it, follow the signs or ask staff once you're inside.

card.hook: Most people head straight up to the top terrace, but the quieter view is halfway down, where a pool of water fills the foreground and the fort and hills rise up behind it. It looks like you planned it, and you didn't.
card.stand_here: Walk to the middle of the garden and stand in front of the water body, right on the phone icon on the map. Face the water so the fort and hills sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the water, fort and hills all in one shot. Try 0.5x if you want more of the garden's edges, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the fort against the hills.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the water along the lower third, then tap the fort and slide the picture a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Aim for late afternoon, around 4 to 5 pm, when you get both day and evening light. Don't plan a shot around the fountains, because they're often not running.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the upper terraces and turn your back on the panoramic view of the garden. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the view fits over your shoulder. The painted palace walls with the Krishna murals also make a fun backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the palace on the uppermost terrace and shoot down over the garden while you stand below, so the whole layout frames you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed, but professional shoots and pre-wedding shoots may need permission, so check on the day. Please don't touch the murals, and take care near the water channels and steps.
card.challenge: Crouch down until the water almost touches the bottom of your screen, then see if you can fit the whole fort on top of it.
card.good_to_know: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built this garden in 1728 as a gift of love for his second queen. She came from the Sisodia Rajput line of Mewar, which is where the name comes from. The double-storeyed palace on the top terrace has galleries and murals showing scenes from the life of Krishna.

card.hook: A castle that's said to be modelled on a Scottish one, perched on a hill above a carved Ganesha temple, in the middle of Jaipur. It's a lovely surprise, and it fits on your phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand in the elevated gardens of Birla Mandir, about 281 m from the Moti Dungri temple, and face north-east. The temple, the fort and the hill all sit together there, with the Jaipur skyline behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the hill, temple and fort into one frame. Switch to 1x for the temple front, then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the fort walls on the hill.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hill or the fort, then slide the picture a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone. Skip Wednesdays if you want fewer people in your photo, because a fair fills the place that day.
card.selfie_here: Try the stairs up to the Moti Dungri Ganesh Temple: face out with the front camera so the fort is behind you. Moti Dungri Road, near the Ganesh temple and Birla Mandir, also works. Hold the phone a bit higher, or use 0.5x, so the castle-style hilltop shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in the raised gardens of Birla Mandir, which give enough distance to fit the temple and fort in one frame, while you stand in front of the temple.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the temple sanctum or near the idol and prayer area, and courtyard rules seem to vary, so follow the signs and any staff instructions. The fort is private and closed to visitors, so shoot it from outside. Drones are generally not allowed around religious sites.
card.challenge: Can you get the temple, the hill and the fort all in one frame without any of them leaning? Turn on gridlines and try to beat your first attempt.
card.good_to_know: The temple was built in 1761 under the supervision of Seth Jai Ram Paliwal. It's in the Nagara style, made of limestone and marble. The fort on top is said to be modelled on a Scottish castle, and that mix of carved stone below and castle walls above is why the spot photographs so well.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the elevated gardens of Birla Mandir, about 281 m from the Moti Dungri temple, and face north-east. The temple, the fort and the hill all sit together there, with the Jaipur skyline behind them.

card.hook: A pale marble arch, an elephant on each side, and a whole sandstone temple glowing behind them. That's the gate at Jagat Shiromani, and it's the reason you'll be glad you stopped in Amer.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the foot of the entrance stairs, in front of the carved marble toran gate, and face the arch head-on. The arch and both elephants will fill your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate straight on. If the whole arch won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the elephants and carvings. Around 2x to 3x is plenty for the carvings, so no need to push further.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the arch up with the centre line, then tap the white marble and slide it a touch darker so the carving stays crisp.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. The sandstone facade has its best light and the gate is quieter, so you get a cleaner shot of it.
card.selfie_here: Climb the stairs and stand beside one of the life-sized elephants so the arch rises behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so more of the gate squeezes in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the temple courtyard facing the marble arch, while you pose in front of the arch with Amer Fort showing beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the outside and the architecture is generally fine, but skip worshippers and the inner sanctum. Photos inside the temple may need a separate ticket, so check on arrival. The staircase is steep, so take care, and keep a firm grip on your phone because there are monkeys about.
card.challenge: Take two matching shots of the gate: one dead-centre and one from a slight angle on the stairs. Then decide which elephant has the better side.
card.good_to_know: Queen Kanakwati, wife of King Man Singh I, had this temple built between 1599 and 1608 in memory of their son Jagat Singh, who died young. It's dedicated to Krishna, Meera Bai and Vishnu, and it's one of the few temples in India where Meera Bai is enshrined beside Krishna. The walls carry carved deities, musicians and floral patterns, so close-up detail shots are worth your time.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the foot of the entrance stairs, in front of the carved marble toran gate, and face the arch head-on. The arch and both elephants will fill your screen.

card.hook: Buses honk, rickshaws weave, and above it all the Hawa Mahal's pink honeycomb front just sits there looking calm. Fair warning: the palace will steal the show from the square, so decide which one you want before you raise your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Badi Chaupar, on the pavement opposite the Hawa Mahal facade, and face north-west. The middle of the square lies a little to the north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the facade above the traffic. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the square and street, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the windows and leave the wires out.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the facade straight against the vertical lines, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early, around 8-9am, when the square is calmest and the facade has its best light. The Hawa Mahal closes after sunset, so evening isn't your friend here.
card.selfie_here: Try a rooftop café across the square from the Hawa Mahal, such as Wind View Cafe. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the facade over your shoulder with the square below in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the pavement opposite the Hawa Mahal facade, aiming back toward the building so the full facade rises above the street.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic in front of the facade is heavy, so keep to the pavement and wait for a gap in the vehicles before stepping out for a shot. Photography at the rooftop café may be for customers only and the rules can change, so ask before you go up.
card.challenge: Get a rickshaw in the foreground with the Hawa Mahal standing perfectly straight behind it, and bonus points if nobody honks at you.
card.good_to_know: Badi Chaupar means "Large Square" and is also known as Manak Chowk. It's one of two major squares built by the King of Amer, with Tripolia Bazar, the city's central market, running between it and its smaller sister, Chhoti Chaupar. The area is still a hub for artisans, jewellers and craftsmen, so there's plenty of street life.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Badi Chaupar, on the pavement opposite the Hawa Mahal facade, and face north-west. The middle of the square lies a little to the north.

card.hook: Most people grab Jal Mahal from the busy main road. Guides say this garden gives you a clearer view, and you get fountains and marble in front of it too.
card.stand_here: Head up to the upper terraces of Kanak Vrindavan, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the subject itself. Face Jal Mahal and Man Sagar Lake, with the fountains and marble work close to you and the Aravalli hills rising behind the lake.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the terraces and fountains, then go to 0.5x to squeeze fountain, lake and hills into one frame. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Jal Mahal on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap Jal Mahal on your screen, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the water and stone.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour is lovely, when the stone glows. Mornings are good too if you like softer light.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the big marble Parikrama fountain in the middle of the garden, the one carved from a single slab, and hold your front camera so the trees and lawns fill in behind you. For something different, stand in front of the Radha Madhav (Old Govind Devji) Temple and let its mirror work and jali-screened walls sit over your shoulder. Fountains aren't always running, so the carved marble is your star either way.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a government-managed garden and temple complex, so entry and photography rules may apply. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a fountain edge or carved arch to sit low in your frame, then see if you can get Jal Mahal peeking out beyond it.
card.good_to_know: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh commissioned this garden roughly 275 years ago as a place of recreation for the royal household. It's named after the Vrindavan of Krishna's stories, and 'Kanak' comes from one of the Maharanis, Kanakde. The main garden has eight sections, and today the Government of Rajasthan looks after it.
